transcript.content:
I've been looking forward to this all week -- it would absolutely make my day if the Moon happened to be visible right now.

I'm in Alice Springs, Australia at 2026-11-10 18:27 ACST (UTC+0930) (2026-11-10T08:57:00Z in UTC), at latitude -23.698 degrees and longitude 133.8807 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 5.086 degrees and its azimuth is 253.378 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 16.793 degrees and its azimuth is 249.764 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 1.32 percent illuminated, 13.169 degrees from the Sun, and 398861.4 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

Probably not with normal unaided eyesight.

Although the Moon is geometrically above the horizon, it is an exceptionally thin crescent—only **1.32% illuminated**—and just **13.17° from the Sun**. More importantly, the Sun is still **5.1° above the horizon**, so the sky around the Moon is bright. At only **16.8° altitude**, atmospheric haze and extinction further reduce the crescent’s contrast.

Under exceptionally transparent conditions, a very experienced observer might conceivably glimpse it after carefully locating it, but for an ordinary observer this would be **extremely difficult and unlikely**. Your chances should improve substantially after sunset as the sky darkens, though the Moon will also be descending and will set fairly soon.

Do not scan near the Sun with binoculars or a telescope while it remains above the horizon.
